reason: Kept on the federal passport guide, which tells people to renew early. Earlier rounds missed that a text sent once a month can reach a date late or not at all when its lead time starts between two runs; the script now lists a row as soon as its lead time will start before the next run, so every row gets at least its full lead time, and the description names the driver's licence that the title promises.
who_trigger_result: Each parent / the monthly job on the 1st, plus a parent's 'file this' or 'did the furnace filter' to add a row or restart an interval / one text listing what is coming due with the official link; nothing is renewed, booked or paid.

demand_source.title: Renew an adult passport | USAGov
demand_source.supports: The federal guide tells people to renew early because processing times vary and some countries and airlines deny entry when a passport has under six months left, which is the case for a long-lead reminder.

edits.description: A monthly text lists what is coming due, with the official link. Each item appears from the last monthly text before its own lead time starts, so it gets at least that much notice (a house choice of about nine months for an adult passport, shorter for a driver's licence, inspection, registration, domains and Global Entry). A child's passport lasts five years and cannot be renewed, so its row says 'apply again in person'. The same table holds each child's yearly check-up, home and car upkeep on a repeat interval (furnace filter, oil change), the end date of a policy or warranty a parent asked Happy to file, and any tax, benefit or gift dates a parent typed in. Nothing is renewed, booked or paid.
edits.how: Preferred build, in the pattern of the model-free watchers (F018): one monthly host command job per parent (`--command-argv`, no model call) runs a reviewed script that reads the dates table generated from family.json5, plus household-store rows (F031) once parents can add them, works out in code which rows to list and prints one templated text, or `NO_REPLY` when nothing is due. A row is listed when its lead time has started or will start before the next monthly run, so every row gets at least its full lead time: a one-week gift date or a domain that renews in three weeks is named in the last text before that lead begins, and is neither skipped nor caught only days ahead between two runs. The 9 Oct build note instead used a monthly isolated automation on the parent's agent with an empty tool list and the table in the job message; that leaves the date sums to the model, so keep it only as a fallback. Rows a parent adds by chat (a filed policy's end date, a typed benefit or gift date, 'did the furnace filter' restarting an upkeep interval) are written to the household store by the parent's own agent.
caveats: The build note has the dates table generated from Tony's registry, which a parent cannot change by chat. The carried-over extras that let a parent add a row ('file this as the car insurance policy', a typed benefit deadline) need either an edit by Tony or the household store (F031) as the table's home; decide which before building.

The text goes out once a month, so timing is to the month and not to the day: a row first appears in the last text before its lead time starts, which can be up to a month earlier than the lead itself. A row a parent adds mid-month with a date before the next run misses the text altogether, so the agent should offer an ordinary reminder (F007) when it files one; a nudge on a particular day is always an ordinary reminder.
Reading a policy PDF to pull out its end date sends that document to the cloud model; whether that is acceptable is still an open decision.
If the fallback is used (a model run with no tools and the table in its prompt), the model works out the lead times itself and can get a date wrong; the script does the sums in code.
Command jobs are created by the operator and run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, so the script is reviewed like the rest of the config repo.

challenge_note: Verdict stands, but the first reviewer's listing rule (lead started, or due before the next run) still gave a date falling just after the next run less than its lead time; the rule is now 'lead time starts before the next run', and the caveat covers rows added mid-month.

demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's own guide gives the health commands, probe endpoints and uptime monitoring as the operator's way to verify that the Gateway and its channels work.

reason: Kept on OpenAI's guidance that whoever deploys an agent should give its user a ledger of what it did and make after-the-fact actions easy to reverse. The build note now names the hook that logs memory saves (they use the built-in write and edit tools, not the in-house tools that keep the journal), the description says undo covers lists, reminders, the calendar and household facts but not a saved note, and a new caveat says that deleting or forgetting a note must also delete its copy in the journal.
who_trigger_result: Each parent, and Tony for forgetting / the Sunday job, a 'what did you do for me?' question, or 'undo that' / one text of what Happy did and saved that week, the last write reversed after a yes, and on request Tony clears what one conversation left in memory.

demand_source.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems (OpenAI), section 4.4 Legibility of Agent Activity
demand_source.supports: OpenAI's guidance says it may be particularly important that whoever deploys an agent gives the user a ledger of what the agent did, as a lighter way than approvals to show a wider range of actions, and that actions reviewed only afterwards should be easier to reverse.

edits.description: Happy records every write it makes for a parent in one journal, so each parent can ask, or read in one Sunday text, what Happy did for them and what it saved to memory that week, and can say 'undo that' to reverse Happy's own last write to a list, a reminder, the calendar or the household facts from the past 24 hours, after seeing what will be reversed. Anything already sent (a text, an email, a print job) cannot be recalled, a saved note is corrected by asking Happy to change it, and clearing what one conversation left in memory stays Tony's job at the Mac, previewed first.
edits.how:
Journal (shared): each in-house write tool (household store, Reminders bridge, calendar write, the reminder-pinning hook) writes a row from inside the tool, where the old value is known: who asked, when, which tool, the inverse call. `openclaw audit --kind tool_action` gives names and outcomes only. Memory saves (F041) are made with the built-in `write` and `edit` tools, not an in-house tool, so their rows come from an observe-only `after_tool_call` hook on those two tools, filtered to the memory files: who, when, which file and the text saved, with no inverse. Approval rows come from the asking hook's `onResolution` callback. Review (G006, F085): a command automation renders the Sunday text with no model; a read tool returns only the asker's rows. Undo (CRT-01): an `undo_last` tool on `

-main`, limited by a `before_tool_call` hook to the requester's rows from the last 24 hours, shows the row, waits for a yes, runs the inverse; for a row with no inverse (a memory save) it says so, and the parent asks Happy to correct or delete the note. Forgetting (F085): `openclaw memory forget --agent --session --dry-run`, then without it, then hand-delete the `curatedWrites` lines.
unverified: Whether turning on message audit rows needs a Gateway restart: the audit CLI page says restart, the Gateway audit page says audit settings apply without one.
Retention for the custom side-effect table in home-store is undefined.
With dreaming switched off (roadmap decision) the session-exclusion setting has little to act on today; its effect was not tested.
The memory-wiki dashboards named on 9 Oct (privacy review, stale pages) are documented, but the plugin is not enabled on this install.
What a forget preview reports on this install was not run; the docs say direct edits are listed for review and are not given per-entry lineage.

That an `after_tool_call` hook on the built-in `write` and `edit` tools is handed the file path and the text written, so that each memory save becomes one dated journal row; this was read in the hook types, not run. Without those rows the weekly list cannot tell this week's saves from older lines in MEMORY.md, which carry no date.
That an approval hook's `onResolution` callback is a workable source for the 'approvals given' line; it was read in the hook reference, not run, and no approval hook exists in the config repo yet.
That no built-in undo for tool effects exists anywhere in 2026.9.7: searches of the installed docs for undo, rewind, revert and checkpoint found none, but the dist source was not read.
Whether the Reminders command-line tool and the calendar server return stable item ids that an inverse can target; neither is installed yet.
caveats: The journal rows for lists, reminders, the calendar and household facts must be written by the write tools themselves from the start, with the old value: rows written by an after_tool_call hook carry no old value and would have to be redone for undo. Memory saves are the one exception: they go through the built-in write and edit tools, are logged by a hook with no inverse, and so appear in the review but cannot be undone.
Sent things cannot be recalled (a text to the other parent, an email to the owner, a print job, a Sonos announcement), so the reply has to say so at the time of sending.

Undo covers only Happy's own writes: if a parent has since edited the same reminder or event on a phone the inverse could overwrite that edit, so the tool should refuse when the item changed after Happy wrote it.

The Reminders bridge (F030) was specified with no delete, so undo adds one, and it must accept only item ids the journal recorded as created by Happy, enforced inside the tool and not left to the model.

Most 'undo' requests are corrections that the same write tool already handles with a second write; undo earns its place for overwritten household facts, where the old value would otherwise be gone, so it is the second step and can be left out without changing the journal or the review.
OpenClaw's own ledger leaves out arguments on purpose, so the in-house table that holds item text and recipients needs a retention limit, which is not yet defined.

Forgetting works per conversation, not per topic: the forget command selects whole sessions, deletes at once unless `--dry-run` is passed, leaves the transcripts, and only lists the notes Happy wrote itself, which Tony then deletes by hand.

The review of actions, the memory list and the week-ahead brief (F014) would otherwise be three Sunday texts to the same parent, so the first two go out as one; lines in MEMORY.md carry no date, so the memory list is reliable only when it comes from the per-write record.

The journal row for a memory save keeps a copy of the saved text in the household store. The forget command does not clean other plugins' stores or backups, so correcting or deleting a note, and forgetting a conversation, must also delete the matching journal rows, or the forgotten text lives on there.
depends_on: F031 household store (holds the journal table)
F041 durable per-person memory (the write path whose saves are reviewed)
An observe-only `after_tool_call` hook on the built-in `write` and `edit` tools, filtered to the memory files (the source of the memory-save rows)
F030 Reminders bridge, with a delete added for undo that accepts only item ids the journal shows Happy created
Message audit rows switched on (`logging.audit.messages`), for the 'texts sent' line

challenge_note: Verdict and the first reviewer's edits stand; added that the new memory-save rows copy note text into a store the forget command does not reach, reconciled the first caveat with the new hook, listed the hook as a dependency, and shortened the anchor to words that sit on one line of the paper.

reason: Kept: the roadmap says Happy stays down after a power cut until Tony unlocks the Mac from home, and 1Password tells its customers to print a recovery sheet and give a copy to someone they trust. Earlier rounds missed that the card calls the pause phrase 'always safe to use' while the stop entry (G005) lets only a command typed at the Mac lift a stop, so a pause by Jordan would last until Tony is home; the card now says so and the choice is listed as a decision.
who_trigger_result: Jordan, with the card prepared by Tony / Happy stops answering while Tony is away, for example after a power cut / a printed page and a sealed envelope that let her unlock the Mac, log in the happy user and restart the gateway, or pause Happy.

demand_source.title: Get to know your Emergency Kit (1Password Support)
demand_source.supports: A shipping password manager tells customers to print a recovery sheet, keep it somewhere safe and hand a copy to a trusted person such as a spouse, so access survives when the owner is unavailable.

edits.how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase, added to the card once G005 is built: sending it harms nothing, but G005 makes lifting a stop a command-line step at the Mac, so the card either carries that step for Jordan or says plainly that a pause lasts until Tony is back. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. The gateway and its helpers are launch agents in the happy user's login session (M0 sign-off), so they start by themselves once happy is logged in and not before. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26 or later, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The commands that may be needed if Happy is still silent: logged in as happy, 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). The house scripts are the operator's repair tools and go with the second envelope: from Tony's admin account 'happy-inspect ready' is a read-only check, while 'happy-deploy --restart' also restarts (ready within about ten seconds at M0) but first applies whatever config is staged, so it is not the card's restart step. (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the nightly backup (its checklist lines are now in G008). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.
caveats: The envelope is a credential on paper. The happy password alone already opens every person's agent data, because the gateway keeps it under that account; an admin credential adds Tony's own account and the config repo. That is the price of not being locked out.
A UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the FileVault screen.
Legacy Contact access needs the access key and a death certificate. It is for the worst case, not for a business trip.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.

The pause is one-way for Jordan unless the card says how to lift it: the stop entry (G005) keeps a stop in a file and makes lifting it a command-line step at the Mac, so the card's restart step is not expected to lift it. Until G005 is built the card has no pause step at all.
depends_on: decision: what goes in Jordan's envelope: the happy user's password only (enough for a restart if it unlocks the disk; it already opens every person's agent data) or also an admin credential (break-glass access that adds Tony's own account and the config repo)
decision: whether Jordan's card carries the step that lifts a stop (G005 makes lifting command-line only, at the Mac) or a pause simply lasts until Tony is back
the existing nightly backup (its checklist lines are now in G008)
a small UPS (already suggested in the roadmap)

challenge_note: Changed keep to edit: the card promised a pause that is 'always safe', but G005 says only a command at the Mac lifts a stop, so the card must either carry that step or say a pause lasts until Tony returns; also 'macOS 26' corrected to 'macOS 26 or later' as the Apple page says.

reason: Kept: OpenClaw's computer-use page tells an operator who does not want screen control to put the command on the Gateway deny list. Two gaps are closed: the 'never enable the Gateway-desktop plugin on the Mac mini' rule gets a posture-check line so it is checked and not only remembered, and the list of commands to keep out of the allow list gains the three the docs name that were missing (camera pan and tilt, sending and searching SMS).
who_trigger_result: Tony as operator / once, now, before any Mac or phone is paired, and again as the off switch during a pilot / a Gateway deny list that withholds screen control, shell, screen viewing and phone-data commands from every paired device, whatever tools an agent is later given.

demand_source.title: Computer use
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's computer-use guide tells an operator who does not want screen control to put the command on the Gateway deny list, and says a denied command is withheld from the device and logged.

edits.how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config, and while no Mac node is wanted also every desktop host command the docs list as arriving with a Mac pairing: `system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, matches exact command names, withholds the command (for `computer.act`, together with the node's `computer` capability) and is logged. The list is Gateway-wide, so the same change carries the phone ceiling for the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): deny the iOS default data commands (`location.get`, `contacts.search`, `calendar.events`, `reminders.list`, `photos.latest`, `motion.activity`, `motion.pedometer`) and the four push-to-talk commands (`talk.ptt.start`, `talk.ptt.stop`, `talk.ptt.cancel`, `talk.ptt.once`), which any node that advertises talk otherwise gets by default and which come off the list only when Talk (VOX-01) is set up; keep every opt-in command the docs list (`camera.snap`, `camera.clip`, `camera.ptz.control`, `screen.record`, `health.summary`, `contacts.add`, `calendar.add`, `reminders.add`, `sms.send`, `sms.search`) out of `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`, and set `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false` so a paired device cannot publish tools to agents. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. Pairing is already manual-only in the config repo since M0 (`gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveLocal: false` and `sshVerify: false`; SSH-verified pairing is otherwise on by default), so keep both and do not use setup links for a Mac, since a setup link can still approve a node's first command surface automatically. The happy-inspect posture check reads only the first of the two; add `sshVerify`, the deny list and `pluginTools.enabled` to it. Leave `gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs` unset (it is off unless set), so no device is approved by network address alone. The deny list covers paired nodes; control of the Gateway's own desktop is a separate route that the docs say needs the `cua-computer` plugin explicitly enabled on the Gateway host, so never run `openclaw plugins enable cua-computer` on the Mac mini, and add a posture-check line that fails if that plugin shows as explicitly enabled, so the rule is checked and not only remembered. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy; device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface; the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals gate shell commands on a node, not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload, with no restart); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility.

challenge_note: Verdict and the posture-check line stand; the opt-in list is completed from docs/nodes/command-policy.md:55, which also names camera.ptz.control, sms.send and sms.search.

who_trigger_result: Tony as operator today, a parent through their own agent later / Tony hands the desk agent one bounded test task (no family task is approved yet) / a short text result, with the screen work confined to a resettable virtual Mac that holds no accounts.

demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents an agent seeing and controlling a paired Mac's desktop through one built-in computer tool as a supported capability.
